lead: Under engine a yacht does not drive like a car: she steers from the stern, slides sideways in the wind and has no brakes. Learn the few forces at work in a marina and you can make them work for you.

qa.q: Why won't my yacht steer when I'm going slowly in the marina?
qa.a: The rudder only works with water flowing past it, from **steerage way** or the **prop wash**. Turn the wheel first, then give a short burst ahead: the wash hits the turned rudder and pushes the stern sideways.

blocks.p: The rudder turns the boat only while water flows past it. That flow comes from the boat's own speed, called **steerage way**, or from the **prop wash**: the stream the propeller throws back onto the rudder. Drifting in neutral, almost stopped, you can put the wheel hard over and nothing happens.

fig.note: The propeller sits just ahead of the rudder

blocks.p: So to swing the bow without gathering speed, turn the wheel first, then give a **short burst ahead**. The wash hits the turned rudder and pushes the stern sideways before the boat starts to move.
Between ahead and astern, **pause in neutral** for a moment so the propeller can slow down. Slamming straight through wears out the gearbox.

blocks.rule: Wheel first, then power. No flow over the rudder, no steering.

qa.q: Which way does the stern go when I put a charter yacht in reverse?
qa.a: To port, usually: most charter yachts have a right-handed propeller, and its **prop walk** kicks the stern to port going astern, strongest from rest with plenty of revs. Berth port side to and the kick pulls the stern in.

blocks.p: A turning propeller also paddles the stern sideways: this is **prop walk**. It is strongest when you engage astern from rest with plenty of revs. Most charter yachts have a right-handed propeller, and it walks the stern **to port** when going astern.

Reversing out of a berth, start gently: as the boat gathers way the rudder takes over and the kick fades. And use the kick where it helps. With a free choice, berth **port side to**: the touch of astern that stops you also pulls the stern in.

labels: a touch of astern to stop

blocks.cap: Port side to with a right-handed propeller: stopping pulls the stern onto the pontoon.

blocks.p: To turn round in a narrow fairway, turn **to starboard**. Put the wheel hard to starboard and leave it there, then alternate short bursts. Ahead, the wash on the rudder pushes the stern to port; astern, prop walk keeps it going the same way.

fig.title: Turning in your own length
lines: Wheel hard to starboard, leave it

qa.q: Why does my stern swing into the pontoon when I steer away from it?
qa.a: Going ahead a boat turns about a **pivot point** well forward, so when the bow turns out the stern swings the other way, into the pontoon. Going astern the pivot point moves aft and the bow swings wide.

blocks.p: A boat does not follow her bow round a corner as a car does. Going ahead she pivots about a point well forward, so when the bow goes one way the **stern swings the other**. Steer away from a pontoon and your stern swings into it.

blocks.cap: Going ahead with the wheel to starboard: the stern swings to port, towards the pontoon.

blocks.p: Going astern the pivot point moves aft, and it is the **bow** that swings wide. Reversing out of a berth and turning the stern to port, watch your bow sweep to starboard across your neighbour.
Astern with a wheel, the **stern goes the way you turn the wheel**. Water now strikes the back of the rudder and tries to slam it hard over, so keep the speed low and hold the wheel firmly.

qa.q: Why does the bow blow off downwind when I slow down under engine?
qa.a: That is **windage**: the keel grips the water amidships, but the high bow has nothing under it, so it blows downwind as you slow. In a crosswind keep just enough speed to steer; to wait, hold her head to wind.

blocks.p: Hull, mast and rolled sails all catch the wind: this is **windage**. The keel grips the water amidships, but the high bow has nothing under it, so as you slow down the bow **blows off downwind**. The slower you go, the sooner it goes.

fig.note: Slowing down: the bow falls off to port, downwind

blocks.p: In a crosswind keep **just enough speed to steer**, no more. Too slow and the wind takes the bow; too fast and you cannot stop when something goes wrong. If you have to wait, turn **head to wind** and hold her there with short bursts ahead: the wind has no side of the bow to push on.
Astern the picture reverses. The bow still blows downwind, so the **stern seeks the wind**. Reversing with the wind on the port beam, wind and prop walk both swing the stern to port.

fig.note: Going astern: the stern swings to port, into the wind

sections.title: Slow in, and ready to go round again

qa.q: How do I come alongside a pontoon when the wind is blowing me off it?
qa.a: Come in at a **steeper angle** and get the bow line ashore at once: a shallow approach lets the bow blow away before a line is on. Approach slowly but still steering, and if a gust pushes you off line, go round again.

blocks.p: Rig fenders and lines, brief the crew and look at the wind before you commit. Approach **no faster than you would be willing to hit the pontoon**: slow, but still steering. When the wind blows you **off** the berth, a shallow approach lets the bow blow away before a line is on. Come in at a steeper angle and get the bow line ashore at once.

fig.note: Wind F4 blowing off the pontoon

blocks.p: If a gust pushes you off line, **abort**: motor clear and come round again. Never let the crew fend off with hands or feet; a fender held on its line does that job.
A **bow thruster** pushes the bow sideways at slow speed. Use it in short bursts with pauses between: run for long, it overheats and cuts out just when you need it.

blocks.rule: If in doubt, go out and come in again.
blocks.label: Remember
